    <title>The dynamics of embolism formation and  repair in xylem conduits: from bubble scale to loss in plant hydraulic  transport capacity</title>
    <abstract>A clear understanding of water usage and resistance to mortality following drought is necessary across tree species. However, despite decades of research, describing plant water movement remains a formidable scientific challenge, and in the absence of this fundamental knowledge, sustainable management of forests will be impossible. All type of plants, including hardwoods and coniferous trees, have core bundles of vascular tissue inside their stems. These circulatory vascular bundles are composed of hollow conduits known as xylem, or wood, that are specialized to transport water efficiently while allowing maximum resistance to drought (hydraulic safety). Sufficient water transport in plants is not guaranteed when water demand increases during hot and dry days. Under those conditions, water in wood becomes highly unstable and trees can die once an air bubble enters and spreads inside those hollow cells. By integrating modelling activities with visual and physiological processes related to air entry and air bubble formation in wood, plant water transport and resistance to drought will be established. The primary impacts of the proposed project will be to advance discovery in the field of water relations and hydraulic architecture of vascular plants by predicting tree mortality following drought, while promoting training for the next generation of scientists and educators. Results from this research can be directly used in future predictions of vegetation responses to climate. The findings here will also be of interest to policy makers, plant breeders and land managers concerned with potential drought impacts on productivity and distributions of certain species.    The overall objective of this project is to link the dynamics of embolism formation and removal under tension in xylem of woody plants starting from the bubble scale and integrating the resulting dynamics along individual conduits to arrive at whole-plant vulnerability to cavitation curves. The specific objectives are to 1) measure and model the timescale required for the gas phase induced by cavitation to fully embolize an entire xylem conduit; 2) investigate the conditions under which bubble formation can spread from one conduit to another; 3) investigate the possibility of bubble resorption under tension to occur; and 4) determine the relation between embolism formation and loss of hydraulic conductivity. To achieve the project objectives, a series of science questions will be addressed: Research question 1 (bubble scale): what are the mechanisms and dynamics of embolism formation and removal in a single xylem conduit? What is the time required for a gas bubble to completely fill and to drain a conduit for varying conduit structures and xylem tensions? Research question 2 (conduit connectivity): Is the time needed for the embolism to fill a conduit dependent on conduit size, and the rigidity of the end-wall pit membrane? Research question 3 (Up-scaling to whole-plant): Do the dynamics of bubble formation in a single conduit explain the whole organ vulnerability to embolism curves. The formulation of bubble formation and spread in transpiring plants will represent a major step forward as the theoretical computational methods, and experimental techniques are now ripe for making this progress.    This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.</abstract>
    <outcomes>The intellectual Merit of the project was to advance discovery in the field of water relations and hydraulic architecture of vascular plants, while promoting training for the next generation of scientists and educators. This project effectively integrated research at different levels of organization from cellular to whole plant by merging experiments, theory, and simulations. The knowledge gained allowed a comprehensive perspective to be formulated that addresses many aspects of plant water storage and resistance to drought.  Water inside plants forms a continuous chain from water in soils to the water evaporating from leaf surfaces. Failures in this chain result in reduced transpiration and photosynthesis and are caused by soil drying and/or cavitation‐induced xylem embolism. This NSF project help determined why variations in xylem network characteristics (such as conduit connectivity) explained trends among woody species, like the ‘safety-efficiency’ trade-off hypothesis. The findings also highlight the picture of the xylem as a complex and delicate conductive system whose hydraulic behaviour transcends a passive gradient-based flow. Finally, these insights provide a better understanding of the existing coordination between the biophysical structure of wood, plant growth, hydraulic partitioning, and physiological plant functions. Although generally overlooked, mechanistic and probabilistic links between vessel anatomical traits and inter-vessel connections were found to be major determinants of vulnerability to drought curve shape and plant resistance to water stress.  Xylem embolism and plant hydraulic failure share several analogies to ‘catastrophe theory’ in dynamical systems. These catastrophes are often represented in the physiological and ecological literature as tipping points when control variables exogenous (e.g., soil water potential) or endogenous (e.g., leaf water potential) to the plant are allowed to vary on time scales much longer than time scales associated with cavitation events. Through this proposal, plant hydraulics viewed from the perspective of catastrophes at multiple spatial scales was considered with attention to bubble expansion within a xylem conduit, organ‐scale vulnerability to embolism, and whole‐plant biomass as a proxy for transpiration and hydraulic function. The hydraulic safety‐efficiency tradeoff, hydraulic segmentation and maximum plant transpiration were examined using this framework. Underlying mechanisms for hydraulic failure at fine scales such as cell wall structure and cell‐wall mechanics, intermediate scales such as xylem network properties and at larger scales such as soil–tree hydraulic pathways were discussed.  The primary impacts of the proposed project was to advance discovery in the field of water relations and hydraulic architecture of vascular plants, while promoting training for the next generation of scientists and educators. The knowledge gained will allow a comprehensive perspective to be formulated that addresses many aspects of plant resistance to drought. This project effectively integrated research at different levels of organization from cellular to whole plant by merging experiments, theory, and simulations. The formulation of bubble formation and spread in transpiring plants represented a major step forward as the theoretical tactics, computational methods, and experimental techniques were ripe for making this progress. Finally, the findings here are also of interest to policy makers and land managers concerned with potential drought impacts on productivity and distributions of certain species. They are also  of interest to tree and plant breeders involved in identifying traits associated with survival and adequate productivity within a given environment.   From this project research, three broader impacts connected global plant functioning to citizen-observable local phenomena through: (1) Engagement of undergraduate and high school students and teachers from North Carolina in cutting-edge research (2) Mentoring three graduate students and one postdoctoral fellow in interdisciplinary research, and (3) Broadening participation among students underrepresented in STEM fields.   In addition, the ideas contained within and the data generated from this project were disseminated through (a) formal seminars at Duke University and the University of Georgia, (b) national and international meetings, (c) over 50 peer-reviewed journals, and (d) the public deposition of hydraulic trait measurements on the  Xylem database and the SAPFLUXNET network.. The broader impacts also lied in the development of mechanistic mathematical models that identified future vulnerabilities of water resources resulting from pine plantation expansion. Results from this research can be directly used in future predictions of vegetation responses to climate change because hydraulic characteristics and their impact on carbon gain and survival is likely a primary determinant of species distributions. Finally, the results also provide guidance for the risk assessment of environment given the strong objectivity of catastrophe theory compared with other evaluation methods. The time is ripe for this undertaking given (i) the proliferation of remote sensing products (NDVI for plants, SMAPS for near‐surface soil moisture, ECOSTRESS for estimating canopy transpiration), (ii) the availability of accessible past, present and projections of large‐scale hydrocli-matic variables (e.g., air temperature and precipitation), and (iii) a wealth of experiments and global public data bases on plant water use (SAPFLUXNET) and hydraulics traits across biomes and species (TRY database and Xylem Functional Trait database).     <title>Distinct photophysics of the spin-entangled triplet-triplet versus free triplets in organic semiconductors</title>
    <abstract>Solar cells absorb sunlight and generate electricity. Solar cells constructed out of organic molecules or polymers are of interest because they are cheap, easily processible, lighweight and flexible. The electric power generated by today's organic solar cells is limited because of thermodynamic constraints. There is currently intense scientific effort to overcome these constraints and to construct solar cells that yield higher power. One possible approach is to use singlet fission, a photophysical process within which the electrical current generated by light absorption is in principle doubled. In this project funded by the Chemical Structure Dynamics and Mechanism (CSDM-A) program of the Chemistry Division, Professor Sumitendra Mazumdar of the University of Arizona is performing quantum mechanical calculations to understand the detailed mechanism of singlet fission. Understanding of the process is needed to find new molecular materials that yield larger amounts of charge upon light absorption, which in turn may lead to organic solar cells with significantly higher efficiencies. The broader impacts of this work include cutting-edge interdisciplinary training of undergraduate and graduate students, and a postdoctoral fellow in computational chemistry and physics. Outreach efforts are fostering interest in chemistry and physics among members of underserved groups.    Currently it is difficult to ascertain whether singlet fission in targeted materials is complete.  The only way to distinguish between the initial optical spin-singlet and the free triplets that are end products, as well as the active intermediate triplet-triplet biexciton is from transient absorption spectroscopy, and transient absorptions in the visible from all three species are overlapping. Experiments in the near and mid infrared need to be performed to distinguish between the different excited species. The project focuses on computations of excited state absorptions from the optical spin-singlet exciton, the lowest spin-triplet exciton and the triplet-triplet biexciton, using high level configuration interaction approach and an exciton basis within a many-electron model Hamiltonian that yield physical, pictorial interpretations of many-body eigenstates and of excited state absorptions. The goal of the project is to develop structure-property correlations with predictive capability of three families of organic semiconductors that are candidates for intramolecular singlet fission. The three families are, (i) covalently linked dimers of acenes and related molecules, (ii) conjugated polymers, and (iii) low bandgap donor-acceptor copolymers. Computations are yielding diagnostic tools for experimentally distinguishing between transient absorptions from the triplet-triplet and free triplets, and determination of whether or not concerted two-electron transfers from the triplet-triplet occur in a bulk heterostructure environment, as has been proposed recently. This research project has implications for solar energy and other technologies that could be based on organic materials.  The students and post-doctoral researchers involved in this project are gaining experience in state-of-the art computational methods, including many-body quantum chemistry and physics treatments.    This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.</abstract>
    <outcomes>Intellectual Merit: The primary goals of the proposed research were (a) to understand the mechanism of singlet fission, which is a photophysical process that in principle can double the quantum efficiency of organic solar cells, and (b) to utilize this understanding to help experimentalists design new singlet fission chromophores that would undergo successful singlet fission more readily. We have made substantial progress in both areas as described below.   Absorption of one light quantum in organics usually generates an optical exciton consisting of one pair of charge carriers, negatively charged electron and posively charged hole which is the absence of electrons. In singlet fission chromophores the optical exciton can in principle dissociate into two lower energy excitons, each of which in principle can yield a pair of charge carriers, thereby doubling the quantum efficiency of charge generation in principle. In reality, the optical exciton decays to a bound state of two lower energy excitons, a biexciton, which then may or may not dissociate into two free excitons, depending on the binding energy of the biexciton. One key problem in the field was to determine whether or not the process of singlet fission was complete, i.e., did the intermediate biexciton dissociate into free excitons or did it stay bound through the lifetime of the experiment? The reason this was difficult to determine was because both the individual lower energy excitons and the biexciton were identified by ultrafast excited state absorption in the visible, where they absobed at nearly the same wavelength, and hence there was no simple approach to distinguish between them.   We have solved this problem. We have shown theoretically that over and above absorbing in the visible, the bound multiexciton should exhibit additional excited state absorption in the infrared, due to charge transfer between the proximate excitons. This knowledge, arrived at theoretically by us, is now being used by multiple experimental groups whose work has not only confirmed the theoretical work, but more importantly, demonstrated that with most real materials singlet fission is not complete, the biexciton is not dissociating and the two exciton components simply recombine.   This brought us to the second phase of our project. Realistic utilization of singlet fission requires that (a) the biexciton is generated in ultrafast times (a few picoseconds) and (b) also dissociates rapidly. There is a catch here in that rapid generation of the biexciton necessarily requires strong electronic coupling between chromophores or chromophore segments occupied by the low energy excitons, which in turn implies strong binding energy. We have solved this problem by interacting closely with two experimental groups who had earlier shown that the solution to the problem lies in working with intramolacular singlet fission compounds in which there occur two distinct kinds of biexciton, - contiguous with strong coupling between proximate excitons, and lower energy biexciton in which the excitons are well separated. Rapid generation of contiguous biexciton followed by downhill transition to the biexciton wirh well-separated excitons with long lifetimes can occur in these cases, as was shown by our experimental colleagues earlier. We have arrived at theoretical proofs for the mechanism suggested by the experimentalists in 2019. One publication with the experimentalists as coauthors has appeared in Nature Chemistry. A theory paper is under review in Physical Review Letters. These results are expected to have a strong impact on the field, as they solve a key conundrum in the field (how to generate weakly bound biexciton rapidly) and will guide future synthesis of new singlet fission compounds.   As of writing this report research involving intramolecular singlet fission compounds containing heteroatoms is in progress.   Broader Impact. Two undergraduate students and two graduate students received extensive training and research experience. One postdoctoral fellow was partially supported by the program. One of the undergraduate students conducted his senior research on singlet fission. He was admiiteed to the graduate program in physics at a prestigious University in 2022. The other undergraduate will graduate in May 2023. One graduate student received his Ph.D. in physics in 2018 and is currently gainfully employed. The other graduate student is expected to receive his Ph.D in May 2024. The Ph.D. theses of both students are based on research supported by this grant. The postdoctoral researcher is currently gainfully employed. Collaborative research was carried out with two experimental groups. Presentations were made at national and international conferences by the PI as well as the graduate and undergraduate students.     <title>Collaborative Research:  Managing oxygen demand in lakes and reservoirs - a competition  between natural and artificial forcing</title>
    <abstract>Abstract    Depletion of oxygen in eutrophic, stratified waterbodies is a significant global problem, which negatively affects drinking-water treatment and cold-water fisheries. Mitigation is increasingly accomplished using oxygenation with bubble plumes. While bubble plumes are successful at adding oxygen, the added energy may induce large-scale mixing, which alters the thermal structure of the reservoir, increases sediment oxygen demand, and changes other sediment-water biogeochemical fluxes (phosphorus, iron, manganese, hydrogen sulfide, and methane). Recent studies of hypolimnetic oxygen demand have shown that oxygen is correlated with the gas flow rate in aerated lakes and that diffusion across the sediment-water interface is greatly enhanced by turbulent episodes generated by seiche currents. Yet, no models exist to predict the currents induced by bubble plumes in crossflow or to relate the turbulent diffusion at the sediment-water interface to the bulk fluid velocity above the benthic boundary layer. Because both of these tools are needed to develop comprehensive models of oxygen dynamics in oxygenated or aerated reservoirs, the purpose of this project is to elucidate the physical mechanisms by which currents resulting from both natural forcing (e.g., inflows and seiches) and artificial forcing (e.g., bubble plumes) affect oxygen demand in lakes and reservoirs.  This goal will be realized through laboratory experiments and field measurements in three different waterbodies. Dye visualization and particle image velocimetry will be used to map the intrusion dynamics for bubble plumes in crossflow. Field experiments will document the intrusion formation and water column dynamics using profiles from conductivity, temperature, and depth (CTD) probes and acoustic Doppler current profilers (ADCP); microstructure at the sediment-water interface will be measured using acoustic Doppler velocimetry (ADV) and temperature and oxygen microsensors.  The PIs will collaborate with a multinational, interdisciplinary team of colleagues from Spain and Switzerland and will pursue three primary objectives: (1) to develop a comprehensive near-field model for plume mixing in stratification and crossflow based on the double-plume integral model approach, (2) to formulate models for oxygen flux across hypolimnetic interfaces due to currents and turbulent mixing by adapting models from film renewal theory, and (3) to integrate the plume and oxygen demand models with a 3D hydrodynamic model, validated using the complete laboratory and field-scale data sets.  The primary intellectual merit will be development of the first scientifically rigorous model for bubble plumes in variable crossflow that includes oxygen transfer between bubbles and water and the formulation of mechanistic models for the flux of oxygen at the sediment-water interface based on ambient currents and turbulence. As an integral part of the research, field experiments will be conducted in three morphologically different lakes, providing a rich archive of data characterizing the intrusion formation from different bubble plumes, the bulk oxygen demand in the hypolimnion, and the benthic mixing. Models developed for these three components (near-field plume mixing, thermocline mixing, and benthic boundary layer oxygen flux) close the gap necessary to develop a comprehensive numerical lake model capable of predicting oxygen dynamics in the hypolimnion of lakes and reservoirs. With several multi-million dollar bubble-plume diffuser installations being considered in the United States, the availability of the coupled 3D lake model will be valuable during design.  The primary broader impact of the proposed activities will be the completed numerical lake model, which will be capable of simulating a wide range of lake oxygen dynamics.  The project leverages the expertise and resources of a multinational, interdisciplinary team of researchers who are leaders in limnology and lake and reservoir management. The results of this research will be disseminated to researchers and managers in an international forum through the International Water Association Specialist Group on Lake and Reservoir Management chaired by the co-PI.  As an integral part of the proposed activities, an innovative program will be developed to mentor graduate students as they develop skills to manage large projects and supervise undergraduates.</abstract>
    <outcomes>Texas A&M University and Collaborating Institution, Virginia Tech, together with foreign partners EAWAG Aquatic Research, Switzerland, and the University of Granada, Spain, have completed research on natural and man-made processes affecting oxygen levels in the bottom waters of lakes and reservoirs.  Oxygen is critical to aquatic life and their habitat and is important to reduce costs of water treatment when reservoir water is used as drinking water supply.  During this project, three field campaigns, two at Carvins Cove Reservoir in Virginia and one at Lake Halwill in Switzerland, were conducted.  These lakes were selected because both of them use engineered bubbles plumes to artificially add oxygen to the lake bottom water and because they span a range of natural conditions, including a wind-protected reservoir at Carvins Cove and an open, alpine lake in Switzerland.  For each field experiment, the project team measured water currents and oxygen concentration near the lake bottom while varying the bubble plume operation.  These field experiments were conducted and analyzed jointly by the full project team.  Specific additional work conducted by Texas A&M University involved two main sets of laboratory experiments, designed to understand the currents that may be generated by bubble plumes in lakes.  These currents are important because they may increase the rate that oxygen diffuses into the lake sediments, where it is consumed by organisms that are decomposing organic matter that settles on the lake bottom.  The first set of experiments studied the detailed flow structure for a bubble plume in a uniform current (see attached Picture 1). The bubbles lift water up in the water column and the currents cause water to translate downstream.  The yellow lines in the figure show the measured pathways of water flowing through and being influenced by the bubble plume.  The second set of experiments focused on the effect of density stratification.  Lakes are stratified due to temperature variation, with cold, dense water at the bottom and warm, light water near the surface.  As bubbles are injected at the bottom of the lake, they drag the cold bottom water upward.  Before this water reaches the surface, however, it falls out of the bubble plume, due to the combined effects of currents and density, generating circulation in the lake bottom waters.  This circulation forces the currents that may ultimately increase the rate of oxygen loss at the lake bottom.  Pictures 2 and 3 show two cases of a bubble plume in weak and strong currents under equal degrees of density stratification.  Several important outcomes resulted from these field and laboratory experiments.  From the lake experiments, detailed measurements of currents and oxygen concentration have allowed us to develop a predictive model for oxygen loss at the lake-sediment interface.  Pictures 4 and 5 show a comparison of the model predictions (Large Eddy Model) with the measurements made during the experiments.  This model is, then, used by collaborators at Virginia Tech and the University of Granada to run numerical simulations of the evolution of oxygen concentration in lakes.   From the laboratory experiments, two main products have resulted.  First, the experimental data has been used to validate (test) the performance of computer models of bubble plumes in stratification and crossflow.  For this work, a new bubble plume model was developed and has been added to a publically-available software package, TAMOC (Texas A&M Oilspill Calculator) which can simulate both bubble or oil and gas plumes in the environment.  Second, the numerical model for the bubble plume has also been added to the lake models developed by Virginia Tech and the University of Granada.  By including the bubble plume and oxygen evolution models in these computer models, we are able to predict the effect bubble plumes will have on lake bottom water oxygen levels.     <title>The Power of Images: A Computational Investigation of Political Mobilization via Social Media</title>
    <abstract>General Abstract  Social media have been described by some scholars as a "weapon of the weak." Any person in the world with a mobile device and network connection can now communicate with a potential audience of unlimited size. This project proposes the first large-scale study of the roll of images in the social media communications of advocacy organizations, social protest movements, and extremist militant groups. The team will collect social media communications in real time and exploit recent "deep learning" advances from computer science to automatically label millions of images for objects (crowds, animals, weapons etc.), entities (specific actors), and emotions evoked (fear, sadness, humor, etc.).  The team seeks to assess whether, all else equal, these images promote political message engagement and diffusion.    Technical Abstract  Research in psychology finds that images are easier for individuals to process cognitively, and have a larger impact on consciousness than do words.   Images should be especially important tools for traditionally marginalized groups that rely on outsider strategies to promote issue awareness and their views. This is new ground however, as there is no theory and no databases for studying the mobilizing effects of political social media communications. The research team will construct new social media databases for a wide range of political groups. The project will contribute new labeled political image collections to existing computer science image repositories. The team also proposes to offer national workshops on advanced image classification methods for social scientists, and will disseminate research findings to scholars and practitioners through conference presentations and peer-reviewed publications.</abstract>
    <outcomes>Vibrant democracies depend on robust political participation. Social media have been described as ?weapons of the weak? because they enable any person in the world with a mobile device and network connection to communicate with an unlimited potential audience. Groups pursuing ?outside? political strategies believe that social media help them to increase issue awareness and promote their views. But how do these groups use social media effectively to advance their causes? We are studying the mobilizing power of images in  social media communications. Psychological research demonstrates that images can have more impact on attention and behavior than words.  We ask whether messaging efforts that include images are more effective, and if so, what types of images are most effective?    This subject of the mobilizing power of images has received little attention to date. We examine it by collecting millions of social media messages in real time from a large number of public organizations and individuals. We then use ?deep learning? methods developed by computer scientists to automatically label the images in these messages for content, before statistically comparing social media messages that were shared more frequently (typically messages related to a salient political issue) to those that were not. We are especially interested in the emotions that images evoke, and which emotions are most likely to lead readers to share a message, or to begin following an organization?s social media account.  Our work on this ambitious project continues and we are grateful for the NSF support we have received.  To date we have published a book to teach other social scientists how to use automated image labeling methods in their own research, and one peer review article examining the effectiveness of social media communications in the wake of the Marjorie Stoneman Douglas High School Shooting. We are currently working on another paper that shows how unsupervised machine learning methods that are commonly used to explore large volumes of text can also be effectively used to explore large image collections.  In terms of broader impacts, our interest in evoked emotions is original and we anticipate that it will inspire follow up research in the field of computer vision methods (where most of the focus to date has been on object recognition). We also expect that our findings will be of value to public organizations that are trying to gain attention to their causes. Finally, this project has created numerous opportunities for graduate student training. The graduate students who have worked on this project are now employed as professors, post-doctoral researchers and programmers. It has also created paid research opportunities for numerous undergraduates, and helped to inspire at least one to pursue a Ph.D.  https://www.cambridge.org/core/elements/images-as-data-for-social-science-research/0376EE8A7A21F5B47FC4EC24DF07EFE9  https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/psj.12410       Last Modified: 10/30/2020       Submitted by: John Wilkerson</outcomes>

    <title>Collaborative Research: Algebra and Algorithms, Structure and Complexity Theory</title>
    <abstract>This project is a collaboration between mathematical researchers at five universities, including young mathematicians at the early stages of their careers, who are joining forces to tackle fundamental problems at the confluence of mathematical logic, algebra, and computer science. The overall goal is to deepen understanding about how to recognize the complexity of certain types of computational problems. The project focuses on a suite of mathematical problems whose solutions will yield new information about the complexity of Constraint Satisfaction Problems. These problems (CSP's) include scheduling problems, resource allocation problems, and problems reducible to solving systems of linear equations. CSP's are theoretically solvable, but some are not solvable efficiently. The research will be aimed at identifying a clear boundary between the tractable and intractable cases, and at providing efficient algorithms for solutions in the tractable cases. Many fundamental problems in mathematics and computer science can be formulated as CSP's, and progress here would have both practical and theoretical significance. A second component of the project investigates classical computational problems in algebra in order to determine whether they are algorithmically solvable. A third component of the project is the further development of the software UACalc, which is a proof assistant developed to handle computations involving algebraic structures.    The researchers shall work to decide the truth of the CSP Dichotomy Conjecture of Feder and Vardi, which states that every Constraint Satisfaction Problem with a finite template is solvable in polynomial time or is NP complete. They will further develop the algebraic approach to CSP's by refining knowledge about relations compatible with weak idempotent Maltsev conditions and about algebras with finitely related clones. A second goal of the project concerns the computable recognition of properties of finite algebras connected with the varieties they generate, such as whether a finite algebra with a finite residual bound is finitely axiomatizable, or whether a finite algebra can serve as the algebra of character values for a natural duality. One of the more tangible accomplishments of this project will be a broadening and strengthening of the applicability of the UACalc software. The agenda for this part of the project includes parallelizing the important subroutines, building in conjecture-testing and search features, adding further algorithms, and further developing the community of users and contributors.</abstract>
    <outcomes>This project was part of five university collaboration of researchers tackling fundamental problems at the intersection of logic, algebra and computer science.  This included developing new techniques in algebra and using them to shed light on problems in computer science.  Conversely, computer science ideas were used to study the complexity of problems in algebra and to improve the speed of certain algorithms in algebra.  This particular project concentrated on the latter and, in addition, the development of a substantial software tool, the Universal Algebra Calculator or UACalc}, used by researchers in the field. UACalc is freely available at http://uacalc.org.  Particular achievements include   A study of which algebras have a  difference term and how to construct one if it exits. There are both  local and global results. It was shown that there is a polynomial  time algorithm to construct such a term in an idempotent algebra, if  one exists.  The algorithm has been implemented in UACalc.    proof that there is no  polynomial time algorithm to test if an algebra has a semilattice  term. This result holds even for idempotent algebras.  On the  other hand testing for an important special kind of semilattice  term, known as a flat semilattice term, is polynomial time for  idempotent algebras.  R. Freese, J. B. Nation, M.     <title>Collaborative Research:   Convergence and Contingencies in Savanna Grasslands</title>
    <abstract>Grasslands and savannas occupy one eighth of the land surface on Earth, are economically important as grazing lands, and are highly impacted by human activities. They also have tremendous conservation value and support most remaining large native grazing animals in the world, particularly in Africa. A fundamental understanding of the factors most important for sustaining savanna grasslands, including their natural fire and grazing regimes, is required for their management and conservation. Scientists have questioned whether grasslands in different regions function similarly. Convergence in functioning would mean that ecological understanding and conservation strategies could be generalized for savanna grasslands worldwide. But contingent factors specific to a region, such as differences in evolutionary history or the types of grazers present, may lead to unique responses in some savanna grasslands. The goal of this research is to compare responses of key ecological processes to fire and grazing in North American and South African savanna grasslands. Scientists will take advantage of three ongoing, long-term experiments that manipulate fire return interval and the presence of large grazers. Responses of plant productivity, plant diversity and nutrient cycling will be compared, and the mechanisms underlying responses, such as differences in plant traits or evolutionary histories, will be assessed.     Comparative research elucidating the consequences of human alterations of fire and grazing regimes worldwide is needed to enable development of management strategies that can insure the sustainability of ecologically and economically important savanna grasslands. This research will provide the basic knowledge necessary to do so, as well as afford training and important global and cultural experiences for young scientists, graduate students and undergraduates. Finally, though collaborations that are already established, results will be made available to scientists and managers in South Africa.</abstract>
    <outcomes>The purpose of this project was to determine the degree of generality we can derive from site-based experimental research. In our case, we wanted to know if savanna grasslands in Kansas, USA,  Kruger National Park, South Africa, and Pietermaritzburg, South Africa responded similarly to key drivers of grassland processes: fire frequency, grazing by native herbivores and interannual climate variability. Knowing this would allow us to determine how much we can generalize the results of our research from one similar ecosystem to another. Overall, we found that ecosystem level processes (net primary production and soil nitrogen availability) responded similarly to fire frequency in Kansas and Kruger. In contrast, some plant community responses differed and others were similar between these geographically disparate systems. For example, grassland biodiversity increased with grazing in both study systems. However, grassland response to fire differed in North America and South Africa. Biodiversity was highest in annually burned grasslands in South Africa and lowest in annually burned sites in Kansas. These differences reflect the much longer history of multispecies of herbivores in Kruger compared to Kansas. Overall, our results showed that many responses between these systems were surprisingly similar despite vast differences in evolutionary history. Therefore, we can detect many generalities in response to common drivers in North American and South African savanna grasslands. This international project presented many opportunities for US students to gain international experience and learn about research in South Africa.     <title>Collaborative Research: Atomic Displacement Engineering of Post-epitaxial Thin-films (ADEPT)</title>
    <abstract>Nontechnical Description: The advent of modern epitaxial semiconductor technologies has resulted in a paradigm shift in optoelectronic and electronic device fabrication. Specifically, the control of semiconductor layer thickness to within a single atomic layer and the creation of multiple, abrupt interfaces between two different semiconductor materials have led to the realization of a host of structures that are key elements in modern lasers, detectors and transistors. However, to date, precise control of chemical composition in heteroepitaxial semiconductor assemblies has been limited to the growth direction - the next leap in the evolution of semiconductor structures will be to realize precise control of composition in all three dimensions, opening routes to optoelectronic building blocks for new technologies, such as quantum computing and cryptography. This project seeks to achieve this goal by using mechanical forces induced by nano-indentation to laterally control chemical composition in semiconductor heterostructures created with existing epitaxial technology. The project integrates experimental measurements of chemical composition and structure at the nanoscale with multiscale computer modeling of atomic diffusion. Using computer models that have been partially informed by specifically tailored experiments, the team explores a broad parameter space and identifies the necessary operating conditions needed to efficiency and robustly drive atomic diffusion. If successful, the outcome of this project could pave the roadmap for creating a new class of semiconductor structures with broad potential applications. The project serves as a multidisciplinary home for training graduate and undergraduate students at both participating institutions. Undergraduate research opportunities for underrepresented groups is a special emphasis whereby students identified at the University of New Mexico are recruited into summer research opportunities at the University of Pennsylvania.    Technical Description: In this project, the research team investigates a new strategy for laterally defining nanoscale compositional patterns in epitaxially-grown III-V semiconductor systems. This multistep strategy is referred to as Atomic-Displacement Engineering of Post-epitaxial Thin-films, or ADEPT, which, coupled with traditional heteroepitaxial methods, may provide a practical pathway for creating three-dimensional quantum barrier configurations with a high degree of controllability. The ADEPT approach employs spatially patterned stress fields and thermal annealing to drive diffusion in a compound semiconductor alloy film comprised of two mobile atomic species with different sizes and diffusional responses to elastic stress. The stress fields are applied by pressing a reusable, pre-patterned array of nanopillars against the semiconductor substrate. Notably, the "press-and-print" ADEPT strategy does not rely on nucleation and growth of sub-phases that are difficult to control and is applicable to any material system in which two mobile atomic species of different sizes are present. The team has recently demonstrated the ADEPT approach in SiGe and here investigates its broader application to III-V heteroepitaxial systems, namely InGaAs and GaAsSb, both supported on InP. In contrast to SiGe, atomic diffusivities in these materials is not fully characterized, particularly as a function of temperature and elastic stress, preventing predictive modeling and the ability to fully explore the ADEPT process. The research activity seeks to overcome the obstacles posed by a large process parameter space and limited experimental throughput with a two-step, computer-aided experimental design approach. In the first stage, data-assisted models are developed using a sequence of relatively "simple" experiments specifically designed to generate information for parameterizing models for interdiffusion in III-V materials. In the second stage, the parameterized models are used to explore the multidimensional parameter space and identify suitable conditions for performing experimental demonstrations of the ADEPT process.    This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.</abstract>
    <outcomes>Heteroepitaxially grown compound semiconductor thin films, namely those comprised of III-V elements, are at the heart of a wide array of devices and technologies, including displays, detectors, and lasers, all of which rely on the ability to create sharp compositional changes in the direction of growth. Interdiffusion of atomic species is a well-known process by which such structures can degrade over time, especially at elevated temperatures. More recently, it has been proposed that controlled and spatially modulated interdiffusion may be used to create more complex structures that are otherwise inaccessible to heteroepitaxial growth. Significant barriers to realizing this goal include the lack of (1) quantitatively predictive models for describing interdiffusion across a broad palette of III-V semiconductor material compositions, and (2) practical methods for spatially modulating interdiffusion that are compatible with III-V heteroepitaxy.  Several facets of these obstacles were addressed in this combined experimental and computational project. First, a new process based on a sacrificial encapsulating layer was developed to increase the fidelity of diffusion data generated by thermal annealing of III-V heteroepitaxial thin films. This process was shown to stabilize the surface of such films during thermal annealing, thereby facilitating the subsequent measurement of subtle compositional changes. Next, a new technique to introduce spatially structured strain fields into III-V semiconductor thin films was developed experimentally, modeled, and parametrically studied. This technique utilizes interdigitated transducers grown on a heteroepitaxial film which, under power, generate surface acoustic waves that induce high amplitude patterned strain fields in the film. Computer modeling of the effect demonstrated that it is possible to introduce strains large enough to substantially alter local atomic mobility in a predictable manner.  These experimental developments were supported by the development of a new mathematical framework for generating continuum descriptions of diffusion. The results of this work led to an improved model for simulating diffusion in systems where the thermodynamics are governed not just by the local composition, but also by local variations. The generalized framework was demonstrated to reduce to the well-known Cahn-Hilliard phase field picture under well defined approximations and should provide a basis for more accurate interdiffusion models. More importantly, it also makes more explicit the connection between experimentally measured data and model parameters, providing a basis for generating predictive interdiffusion models for a broad range of material systems.     <title>High-speed and minimally photo-damaging STED microscopy using nanolaser arrays</title>
    <abstract>This project will develop a fast, affordable, and miniaturized microscopy system to image the fine ultrastructure of cells, with minimal photodamage or photobleaching of fluorescent probes.   Success of this proposal will significantly advance the field of microscopy, specifically super-resolution fluorescence imaging. The development of high-performance, fast, compact and affordable microscopes will impact medical diagnostics such as cancer and Alzheimer's disease.       The principal investigator will develop the next generation of stimulated emission depletion (STED) microscopy for high-performance, fast, compact and affordable STED microscopes. The PI will integrate metallic nanolaser arrays into STED systems which will greatly improve imaging speed and reduce the size and cost of the equipment    This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.</abstract>
    <outcomes>Super-resolution fluorescence microscopy can visualize subcellular structures with below 200 nm spatial resolution and it has revolutionized fundamental biology and biomedicine. STED microscopy is one of the super-resolution imaging techniques and has been widely used due to its easy-to-use. However, it has several drawbacks including slow imaging speed, high illumination intensity and high cost. The objective of the proposal is to study the prospect of developing the next generation STED microscopy that might be able to overcome some of its shortcomings by replacing bulky, expensive and noncontrollable laser system with a novel type of light sources based on nanolaser arrays.  There were some of our findings/outcomes:  We developed a metallic nanolaser emitting at 785 nm which is suitable for STED microscopy. We found an optimal recipe for the fabrication of the nanolaser. We developed multiline excitation and detection imaging system which significantly reduces photobleaching and photodamage of the biological samples. We developed deep learning network for denoising STED images, which substantially improve signal-to-noise ratio of images.   We expect that our new STED imaging system will allow ones to carry out fast and gentle 3D super-resolution imaging in living cells. However, we also found that there are still technical challenges in fabricating nanolaser lasers, which is possibly overcome by further optimization and development of recipes.     <title>BSF:2014170: SINR-Governed Wireless Networks: Geometric Analysis and Algorithms</title>
    <abstract>Among many different models used to describe wireless networks, the PIs will focus on the one commonly called the SINR (Signal-to-Noise-and-Interference Ratio) model.  It attempts to model the reception or non-reception of a wireless transmitter signal in the presence of interference from other transmitters and ambient noise. Much recent work has been devoted to analyzing the SINR model and using it to predict the behavior of real-life wireless networks.  One simple aspect of this model is the construction of a SINR reception map, which associates with every transmitter the region where it can be received and also contains a region where no signal can be received due to interference of multiple transmitters.  The exact map is difficult to compute due to the complexity of the so-called SINR inequality that determines whether or not a signal is received. Previous work has been done on approximating the reception map.  The methods for this computation suffer from slow construction times (so-called preprocessing times) and from the fact that, for transmitters of unequal power, the preprocessing time depends not only on the number of transmitters and the accuracy of the approximation, but on other parameters of the problem that can not be expressed in terms of these two.  The PIs will develop methods to overcome these by speeding up the preprocessing times.    More specifically, the PIs will develop batch preprocessing for SINR-diagram point location queries.  They will then use these tools to speed up existing algorithms for SINR-governed wireless networks. The PIs will study fundamental problems arising in SINR-governed wireless networks, combining algebraic tools with techniques of computational geometry and combinatorial optimization. The PIs will investigate a diverse suite of problems, including how to cope with directional antennas, problems arising when successive interference cancellation is enabled, combinatorial problems concerning SINR diagrams, and combinatorial optimization problems such as scheduling under a restricted, more practical version of the SINR model.  The PIs will also investigate further applications of the underutilized combination of computer algebra and computational geometry tools in a more general context.    Understanding the geometric properties of SINR-governed networks and being able to analyze such networks and predict their behavior is extremely important.  Moreover, efficient solutions to the problems of this family, as well as to problems that PIs intend to study from a more practical point of view, will benefit the motivating application domain of wireless communication. These solutions are essential in the planning stages of such networks (e.g., determining where to locate the devices), for examining existing networks, and for utilizing them efficiently. In this respect, the proposed project has the potential for substantial socioeconomic impact, as the popularity of such networks is rapidly increasing.    The project incorporates an educational mission, through training of graduate students and reciprocal visits among students and participants from the two institutions.</abstract>
    <outcomes>This NSF grant is a companion to the BSF grant 2014/170 "SINR-Governed Wireless Networks: Geometric Analysis and Algorithms".  This document summarizes the outcomes of the two grants.  The Israeli Co-PI on the BSF grant is Matthew (Matya) Katz of Ben-Gurion University.   The SINR (Signal to Interference plus Noise Ratio) model attempts to more realistically predict whether a wireless transmission is received successfully, in a setting of multiple simultaneous transmitters and background noise, taking into account the attenuation of electromagnetic signals.  While much previous research focused on the implications and the properties of this model, relatively little work was devoted to efficiently answering basic questions in this setting.  In contrast, one of the main objectives of this project was to devise compact data structures for predicting whether one of the transmitters is received at a given query position and, if yes, which transmitter.  This objective has been attained.  We have described and analyzed data structures for such queries in several settings.  We started by presenting a very efficient batched algorithm, which solves the problem for a large number of simultaneous receiver locations.  We used a rarely-employed combination of algebraic techniques with conventional range-searching data structures.  This approach promises to be more universally applicable.   We then considered the more challenging version of the problem, where the transmitters are preprocessed to facilitate quick individual reception queries, and the setting is dynamic: transmitters can be added or removed over time, with the data structure updated efficiently.  The data structures handle both the case of uniform transmitter power (all transmitters are at the same power level) and non-uniform transmitter power (transmitters may transmit at different power levels).   All of our data structures are optimal up to logarithmic factors, except for one situation: dynamic data structure to handle the non-uniform power case.   We then constructed a dynamic data structure to solve a problem not heretofore addressed in the literature, to the best of our knowledge: Given a collection of sites with positive weights, say in the plane, facilitate multiplicatively weighted nearest-neighbor queries.  This involves identifying the site that has the closest distance to the query position, with the distance multiplied by the site's weight.  While additive weights are commonly handled, there does not appear to be a dynamic (i.e., allowing addition and removal of sites) data structure for handling multiplicative weights.  We constructed such a structure with optimal space, preprocessing, query time, and amortized update time, within logarithmic factors.    The data structure described above was then used to settle the remaining dynamic SINR query problem, namely that of non-uniform transmitter powers, in time, space, query time, and amortized update time optimal within logarithmic factors.   Intellectual Merit  The work formulated provably efficient (optimal within logarithmic factors) algorithms for answering essential questions in the SINR model of wireless networks.  A number of other geometric questions were studied as well, with significant progress made in geometric algorithm design.  Algebraic techniques we used will have further applications in computational geometry.  Broader Impacts  The results of the work were presented at major conferences and competitive archival journals.  Several PhD and MS students and a postdoctoral associate were trained while participating in this research.  The tools developed in this project will prove useful in efficient simulation and optimization of SINR networks.  The multiplicatively weighted nearest-neighbor data structure for dynamic data will find applications in a wider context of geometric computation.     <title>Doctoral Dissertation Research: The Construction & Circulation of Do-It-Yourself (DIY) Music Technology</title>
    <abstract>Introduction    This project examines the practices of musician-inventors in Berlin, Germany who build and modify musical equipment. Specifically, it is an ethnographic study of how networks of Do-It-Yourself (DIY) music technologists are formed and how their structures, ideas, and building processes contribute to larger discourses about the invention, use, and repurposing of technologies. The research will bring together interdisciplinary approaches to music, technology, and society with new participant observation, interviews, and data collection. The overarching purpose is to provide a cogent account of independent innovation in contemporary sonic arts. DIY music technologists and the objects they create are entwined in socio-technical systems from which many paths and outcomes have yet to be explained. The central research question here is to determine how sound technologies, creativity, and knowledge production are linked and potentially transformed through the DIY process.    Intellectual Merit    This study investigates where the contemporary DIY ethos fits within the historical trajectory of hobbyism, amateurism, sound recording and production, and artistic and technological innovation, establishing what is unique about this specific, post-internet, post-globalization juncture. The topic probes the real-world usefulness of notions such as expertise, knowledge production, and innovation, as well as questioning barriers to access and education about technology. Viewing DIY music technology through the frameworks of Hacking and Folk Technology can contextualize this phenomenon within a broad range and scale of participating communities, revealing insights into human-technology interaction.    Potential Broader Impacts    The research may have broad implications for issues of circulation, access, and agency worldwide, as both non-Western metropolitan sites and increasingly connected rural sites share and create new modes of social interaction involving sound and technology. This new comparative study in Berlin complements a prior three years of research in New York City and ideally precedes further fieldwork in non-Western settings as part of the researcher?s long-term commitment to exploring nontraditional partnerships for connecting technology with the arts. Ultimately, the project aims to provide an entry point for understanding technologies in various geographical regions and contexts.</abstract>
    <outcomes>From Occupy Wall StreetÆs opprobrium for financial excess to former NSA contractor Edward SnowdenÆs release of confidential U.S. government documents on the basis of ethical objection, myriad forms of resistance and protest have grabbed recent media headlines and captured the public imagination. Yet beneath the radar of popular news coverage, another form of resistance is brewing in the realm of technology and the arts, linking the history of technical invention with current events in the early 21st century. This research project is an ethnomusicological investigation of "DIY (Do-It-Yourself) music technologists," a loose network of musician-inventors independently constructing instruments and sound technologies outside the context of large musical equipment corporations. DIY music technologists disrupt formal channels of production and consumption, actively reasserting the agency of individual creators and challenging notions of expert knowledge. The study examines how this phenomenon affects human-technology relationships by bridging the social, technical, and aesthetic realms through ethnographic fieldwork conducted in Berlin and New York City, two international hubs for music technology widely recognized by participants.  Following prior New York fieldwork, the Co-PI worked with musician-inventors in Berlin, Germany during the NSF-supported research stage. The Co-PI conducted extensive interviews with musical instrument builders, received technical instruction through workshops alongside other amateur-to-intermediate builders, charted the connections between coworking/hacker spaces and underground music scenes, attended relevant concerts and lectures, and conducted frequent participant observation at community sound arts venues. In doing so, the researcher was able to survey the changing urban geography and governmental policies affecting local artistic practice; the physical and virtual circulation and potential for mobility of people, objects, and ideas; the economics of DIY movements; the relationship between gender and participation in electronic arts workshops; and the historical implications of experimenting with music and electronics from the former East Germany through the present.  Key findings include:  -   The Co-PI discovered a network of people, objects, and ideas linking not only Berlin and New York, but also international musicians who come to the city due to its inexpensive rent and cultural orientation. Such patterns of economic migration include those moving from and between Berlin and London, Scandinavia, the Czech Republic, and Latin America.  -   Besides interviews, workshops conducted by musician-inventors proved a primary site for gathering information. These included entire days spent learning how to build experimental instruments, including the "micro_blackdeath noise synthesizer," the "soundbox," and the "microgranny." The most prominent venue for such workshops was the sound arts venue NK Projekt.  -   Despite the diversity of the movement, certain objects, events, and terms were found to be central to participation. For example, knowledge of the Arduino microcontroller, BerlinÆs winter Transmediale and CTM festivals, and the concept of "hardware hacking" would commonly mark someone as a DIY music technologist.  -   Observations of gendered participation indicated that discourses and performances of masculinity are often rewarded for both males and females (with queer perspectives absent and femininity downplayed); female participation is rising but was found to stagnate after the introductory level; a critical, local dialog on female and feminist perspectives was stronger in the related media arts than in music technology, although some initiatives to promote female musical participation were identified.  -   An unprecedented number of new technology start-up companies, coworking spaces, and fabrication laboratories (the largest being the venue Betahaus) figured into the DIY music technology ne...</outcomes>

    <title>NCS-FO: The evolutionary origins of leadership in chimpanzees: from individual minds to collective action</title>
    <abstract>Leadership is crucial for effective cooperation, especially in large and complex groups. Yet there is an empirical and theoretical gap in our understanding of the individual-level processes underpinning leadership and the group-level consequences of leadership. How does the cognition of individual leaders translate into coordinated group action in the real world?  This project proposes using chimpanzees as a new model of human-like leadership to better understand the evolutionary origins of our own leadership patterns. We will bridge the gap between individual- and group-level phenomena by conducting matched research with semi-free ranging chimpanzees living in a sanctuary where we can do detailed assessments of cognition, and with chimpanzees living in the wild where we can look at complex group behavior in a natural setting. By matching datasets across these two contexts, we will be able to see how individual cognitive process translate into group action. While humans are thought to be uniquely able to establish leadership through prestige and collaboration instead of just pure physical domination, chimpanzees are our closest living relative, also show variation in how individuals obtain and maintain status in their groups. This project will therefore illuminate the evolutionary origins of human leadership, and also set a new agenda in evolutionary cognitive science for studying cognition in the wild. Training, education, and outreach from elementary school through to graduate school will be integrated throughout the project both domestically and abroad. As part of this proposal, we will develop a leadership module for children, using animal models to demonstrate different forms of leadership. We will implement this module through outreach at local schools and museums in the US and in 16 primary schools in Uganda. Undergraduates and high school students in the US will gain hand-on research experience through internships and in coursework. Two postdoctoral researchers and a graduate student will further gain international research experiences in the course of the project. This integrated approach to research and education will train a new generation of evolutionary cognitive scientists and disseminate primate research to the public.    This project has three specific aims. The first aim is to identify individual leaders (those with outsized influence) in natural social groups across multiple contexts of behavior including dominance rank, initiation of group movements, resource acquisition, within-group mediation and inter-group aggression. The second aim is to create leadership profiles by characterizing individual variation in the cognitive, behavioral, and physiological mechanisms of leaders across these contexts. At the sanctuary, 100+ chimpanzees across 5 social groups will be assayed for cognition (including social cognition, cooperation, and executive function); temperament; behavior (aggression and affiliation), and physiology (hormones and body size) to predict leadership. At the field site, similar assessments will be made of temperament, behavior, and physiology, drawing on a longitudinal database with 30 years of data on 150 wild chimpanzees. These data will be used to test the hypothesis that there are distinct pathways to leadership in chimpanzees, with intimidation-based and cooperative strategies being the most important, but knowledge and motivation anchoring some forms of leadership. The final aim is to understand how variation in leadership styles shapes the outcomes of collective action by examining several short-and long-term metrics of leadership success, including group cohesion, rewards received, and biological outcomes like reproductive success that can only be studied in the wild. This project will bridge individual-level and group-level perspectives on cognition, behavior, and physiology by leveraging the strengths of two natural populations of chimpanzees. The project will match experimental and observational techniques across sites on a scale never previously done, and will develop chimpanzees as a new model for human leadership.    This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.</abstract>
    <outcomes>Goals & Activities: The University of New Mexico, in collaboration with Tufts University and the University of Michigan, generated novel findings on leadership in chimpanzees, humans closest evolutionary relatives, the results of which shed light on the evolutionary origins for unique patterns of prestige and social cooperation in humans. While leadership in most nonhuman animals is strongly dependent on the ability to physically dominate others, humans are exceptional in the degree to which leadership may arise from other routes, involving diverse individual strategies and their associated neurocognitive mechanisms. Our research aimed to identify alternative strategies for social influence across the domains of chimpanzee social behavior. We used a novel design to connect lines of evidence from naturalistic observations of social behavior to minimally-invasive controlled cognitive experiments in both wild groups and semi-free-ranging groups housed in African sanctuaries. To achieve these aims, the University of New Mexico led the collection of over 13,000 hours of naturalistic field observations of social behavior of wild chimpanzees in the Kibale National Park, Uganda. Additionally, through UNMs Comparative Human and Primate Physiology Center, we analyzed over 7,000 biospecimens collected non-invasively from wild and sanctuary-living chimpanzees to assess hormones that have been associated with temperament, social tolerance, and leadership styles in humans.   Outcomes: Whereas aggressive competition has been recognized as the primary determinant of social status in chimpanzees, our research revealed alternative forms of leadership in individuals who are not at the top of the dominance hierarchy. First, particular chimpanzees exhibited leadership in the context of high-risk cooperative behaviors, such as hunting. While these males were not necessarily more skilled than others, their participation enhanced group success by promoting the cooperation of others. Second, when past their physical prime, many male chimpanzees invested in strong political alliances that buffered them from the loss of social status with age. These prosocial strategies, which were associated with reduced aggression, allowed males to sire offspring and maintain strong social integration until later in life than is observed in other primates, with the exception of humans. Our study also helped explain sexually-differentiated patterns of cooperation and identified social tolerance as a critical ingredient for cooperation in female chimpanzees. We developed novel approaches for characterizing individual variation in hormonal profiles and associated this variation with social behavioral styles exhibited by wild chimpanzees, as well as with performance of sanctuary chimpanzees on cognitive tasks measuring risk-taking and impulsive decision making. Hormonal studies also described chronic physiological costs associated with conventional aggression-based status competition, a factor which likely promotes alternative leadership pathways. While phenomena such as prestige-based leadership are not fully developed in apes, the advances from this study identify some shared features and mechanisms associated with leadership behavior in chimpanzees and humans and localize these features in the unusual degree of cooperation exhibited by both species. The funding resulted in 11 publications in high-impact journals including Science, Science Advances, Hormones and Behavior, Journal of Experimental Psychology, and Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society.   Broader impacts: The collaboration enabled students and postdoctoral scholars to gain interdisciplinary training and cross-mentorship across the three institutions. The principal investigators and their trainees developed the Primate Learning in Action website (https://sites.lsa.umich.edu/primatelearning/) to disseminate information about primate cognition, behavior, and conservation at a range of knowledge levels. Examples from this research were used to develop modules on data collection and analysis, and curated media from the investigators to communicate study findings. The study supported 15 Ugandan field researchers and support staff at the Kibale Chimpanzee Project to coordinate the daily data collections and primary data entry, providing specific training to carry out the study protocols and broader professionalization opportunities through peer mentorship across performance sites and community engagement. The investigators served continuing roles as collaborators and advisors for donor-supported partner projects that serve the educational and conservation needs associated with our research presence in rural Uganda. These include the Kasiisi Schools Project, the Kibale Snare Removal Project, and the Chimpanzee Health Intervention and Monitoring Program, which operate a variety of education, conservation, and health programs in and around Kibale National Park in collaboration with the local communities and wildlife authority. These programs have collectively reduced the occurrence of poaching and resulting injuries to chimpanzees and improved attitudes to wildlife both directly, through programming in 16 local schools, and indirectly, by linking community development and educational programming to the conservation of wildlife. Our research and conservation arms are collaborating on the Healthy Children Health Chimps program that coordinates efforts to monitor and study disease outbreaks in local communities and in chimpanzees to reduce disease transmission. The results of these efforts were critical for reducing the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic.        Last Modified: 12/10/2023       Submitted by: MelissaThompson</outcomes>

    <title>AF: Medium: New Frontiers in Equilibrium Computation</title>
    <abstract>Concepts and methodologies from economics and social sciences have found numerous applications in the study of the Internet and e-commerce.  At the core of many such applications lies the notion of equilibria, which has been widely studied by game theorists and economists to model and predict the strategic behavior of selfish yet rational agents.  During the past decade, the computation of equilibria in both games and markets has been studied intensively and many of the exciting developments have brought new insights towards a much better understanding of equilibria.  At the same time, they opened up a window to many new research challenges.  The goal of the project is to explore some of the important directions and problems that have emerged in the new frontiers of equilibrium computation.  Research along directions pursued in the project will complement the already extensive literature in economics and social sciences on equilibria, by offering new perspectives through the lens of algorithms, approximation, and computational complexity.  In addition to curriculum development, mentoring PhD students, and involving undergraduate students in accessible projects, the PIs will actively pursue outreach activities and broadly disseminate results obtained in the project.    Some of the research directions that the PIs plan to explore include the following:  1) Deepen our understanding of the new exponential-time hypothesis for fixed-point computation employed by Rubinstein in his recent breakthrough, by exploring its connections with other natural conjectures on the exact complexity of fundamental equilibrium computation problems.  2) Explore connections between two problems that have been studied intensively in the literature, the problem of finding an approximate Nash equilibrium in an anonymous game with a polynomial precision and that in a two-player game with a constant precision.  3) Study the computation of equilibria in games and markets with a unique equilibrium.  Equilibrium as a prediction tool is more meaningful when a unique equilibrium exists.  4) Work towards a dichotomy theorem for Arrow-Debreu market equilibria that aims to classify every family of utilities into those that are easy to solve and those that are intractable.</abstract>
    <outcomes>The notion of equilibria plays a central role in the modeling of interactions between rational agents each with their own objectives. The project investigated algorithms for the computation of equilibria in a variety of settings and the complexity of the associated problems. Below we describe some of the main results achieved.  In the one-sided matching problem, we want to match agents to goods, given the utilities of the agents for the goods. A classical scheme proposed by Hylland and Zeckhauser in 1979 uses the power of a pricing mechanism to derive a randomized allocation that has several desirable properties, e.g. is envy-free (no agent prefers the allocation of another agent) and is Pareto optimal. We addressed the computational complexity of the problem of computing a solution in the HZ scheme. We presented a strongly polynomial-time algorithm for the case when the agents' utilities come from a bivalued set. In the general case, we classified the complexity of the HZ scheme and showed that computing an approximate HZ equilibrium is intractable, according to current complexity assumptions.  We studied the pacing equilibrium problem for budget management in online auctions. To manage budget constraints and smooth out the expenditure across auctions, the bidders (or the platform on behalf of them) often employ pacing: each bidder is assigned a multiplier between 0 and 1, and her bid on each item is multiplicatively scaled down by the multiplier. We showed that the problem of finding an approximate pacing equilibrium (assignment of multipliers) is intractable.  We studied traffic equilibrium problems in the presence of autonomous vehicles as rational players using an approach based on mean field games. We developed an algorithm for finding an approximate equilibrium in a mean field traffic flow problem based on the multigrid preconditioned Newton's method. We furthermore presented scalable traffic stability analysis for both pure autonomous vehicle traffic and mixed traffic (with both autonomous and human-driven vehicles) based on mean field games. It is shown from linear stability analysis and numerical experiments that autonomous vehicles help stabilize the traffic.  We developed polynomial-time algorithms for the qualitative reachability analysis of branching concurrent stochastic games, a class of infinite-state, imperfect information stochastic games that generalize several other stochastic games and models (e.g. finite-state concurrent games, branching simple stochastic games). Algorithms were developed both for the almost-sure reachability problem and the limit-sure problem, i.e. determining whether there is a policy that reaches the goal with probability exactly 1, or arbitrarily close to 1, and computing such a policy.  We studied the proportional allocation rule used in proof-of-work blockchains, where each miner for one completed block is awarded by an amount that is, in expectation, proportional to the number of hashes the miner contributed to the mining of the block. We presented an axiomatic theory of incentives in proof-of-work blockchains at the time scale of a single block.    Algorithms and lower bounds were obtained for a number of other problems, including in particular problems in smoothed analysis and property testing. Highlights include the following: Improved smoothed analysis of the FLIP algorithm for the Local Max Cut problem on general graphs. An optimal algorithm and matching lower bound on the query complexity of testing whether an unknown Boolean function is unate (i.e. every variable is either non-decreasing or non-increasing) or is far from unate. Algorithms and lower bounds for population recovery from the deletion channel, i.e. learning an unknown distribution over an unknown set of bit-strings, given access to independent draws from the distribution that have been corrupted by deletion of bits with some fixed probability. Optimal algorithm and matching lower bound for estimating the number of edges of an unknown undirected graph with access to an independent set oracle.
